newsitem.title: USA: Leaf rust 'widespread' in U.S. HRW wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: Leaf rust 'widespread' in U.S. HRW wheat crop.

text.p: Widespread incidents of leaf rust fungus in U.S. hard red winter wheat could lower yields and quality next spring if it is not destroyed by freezing winter temperatures, crop experts said Wednesday.
"We just have an extremely widespread epidemic right now," said Merle Eversmeyer, research plant pathologist with the U.S. Agriculture Department's Agricultural Research Service in Manhattan, Kan.
Experts said damage to wheat yields and quality will not occur unless the leaf rust spores "overwinter" -- that is, manage to survive through the winter.

"In this central Plains area -- from southern Nebraska to northern Texas -- we normally do not have a severe or economic loss from leaf rust unless we've had leaf rust overwinter," Eversmeyer said. "If anything allows those leaves that are infected to survive, then the rust survives."

Eversmeyer said a weather model that he uses to forecast the early spring survival of leaf rust suggested that there will be some overwintering this year, especially in Kansas and northern Oklahoma. He added that the model usually had a 70 percent accuracy rate at this time of year.
Rollie Sears, a wheat breeder at Kansas State University Research and Extension in Manhattan, estimated that at least 60 percent of the Kansas crop was infected with leaf rust.
"We just have to take it as a potential warning. When we have leaf rust overwintering from fall infections, generally we have pretty severe leaf rust epidemics the following spring," Sears said.

Leaf rust reduces wheat quality by lowering protein concentration. If the infection occurs early enough in the spring, it can also lead to yield reduction by cutting off the plant's ability to nourish itself.

Sears said that not only have favorable fall moisture and temperatures allowed Kansas HRW wheat to get off to a strong start, they have also permitted fungal diseases such as leaf rust and septoria and viruses such as leaf streak to develop.
Sears said that leaf rust survived the winter of 1994-1995 and Kansas had a severe problem in the spring.

State crop reports released Tuesday showed that U.S. winter wheat was 89 percent emerged during the week ended Sunday, compared with 85 percent during the previous week, 83 percent the previous year and 83 percent for the average.
